clinical_category: Glasgow Coma Scale - confounders and safe interpretation
blueprint_topic: Reducing diagnostic error when treatment or physiologic factors limit neurologic assessment
stem: A mechanically ventilated client with acute brain injury has received sedating medication. Which nursing interpretation of the Glasgow Coma Scale is most appropriate?

options.A: Document the eye, verbal, and motor findings with assessment limitations and consider intubation and sedation before interpreting a lower score as neurologic deterioration
options.B: Treat any decrease in total GCS as proof of worsening brain injury because medications and intubation do not affect the scale
options.C: Omit the motor and eye components because intubation makes the entire GCS unusable
options.D: Use the total GCS alone because pupillary and other neurologic findings are unnecessary when a score is available

rationale: A is correct. The current 2026 NCBI/StatPearls Glasgow Coma Scale chapter identifies intubation as a limitation of verbal scoring and sedation as a potential confounder that can depress GCS findings. Hypoxia, hypotension, intoxication, and other physiologic or treatment-related factors can also alter the score. The source recommends documenting the individual eye, verbal, and motor components and recognizes that GCS does not assess pupillary responses or brainstem reflexes. Therefore a lower total score must be interpreted in clinical context rather than automatically attributed to neurologic deterioration. B ignores verified confounders. C unnecessarily discards assessable components. D overstates the completeness of the total score.
educational_objective: Interpret GCS results in clinical context by documenting individual components and recognizing that intubation, sedation, and physiologic disturbances can confound the score and do not replace a broader neurologic assessment.
source_version_date: StatPearls 2026 Internet edition; last updated 2026-04-19; accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: NCBI Bookshelf 'Glasgow Coma Scale' → Issues of Concern → Factors That May Interfere With GCS Assessment: sedatives can depress GCS; intubation limits verbal scoring; hypoxia and hypotension can confound scores; sedation or pharmacologic paralysis may further confound assessment. Physiologic/neurologic limitations: GCS does not assess brainstem reflexes or pupillary responses. Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes: nurses document eye, verbal, and motor components individually followed by the total score for trend monitoring.
source_claim_supported: The current April 2026 StatPearls chapter directly supports contextual interpretation of GCS when intubation, sedation, hypoxia, hypotension, or other factors limit component assessment and supports separate component documentation.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential client-needs subcategory (9–15% of items); this item tests safe interpretation of diagnostic/assessment data and recognition of factors that can produce misleading results.
correction_summary: Total duplicate-avoidance rebuild. The source item's simple eye/verbal/motor component question duplicated information already embedded in V2-Q1983. The final item uses the same current 2026 GCS authority but tests a distinct Reduction of Risk Potential construct: recognition and documentation of intubation/sedation and physiologic confounders that can distort GCS interpretation.
audit_findings: The original generic AAN component-identification item duplicated GCS information already used in V2-Q1983.
Current April 2026 StatPearls directly identifies intubation, sedation, hypoxia, hypotension, and other factors as GCS confounders or component limitations.
The final item preserves use of assessable GCS components rather than declaring the whole scale invalid in an intubated client.
The item explicitly prevents a lower total score from being treated as proof of neurologic deterioration without clinical correlation.
Independent adversarial second pass found one uniquely correct interpretation, no second defensible option, no unsupported scoring substitution, no cueing, and no unresolved conflict.
